a OurBigBook.com
The Laurent series is
e−1/z=∑n=0∞​n!(−1)n​z−n=1−z1​+2z21​−6z31​+⋯,z=0.
(1)
Its principal part contains infinitely many nonzero negative powers, so zero is an essential singularity. The first three displayed terms are not an asymptotic truncation as z→0; they are the beginning of the convergent Laurent series in powers of 1/z.

Words: 31 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 31
b OurBigBook.com
The coefficient of z−1 in the Laurent series is −1. The residue theorem therefore gives, for the standard positive orientation,
∮C​e−1/zdz=2πiResz=0​e−1/z=−2πi.​
(2)
The residue theorem applies to an isolated essential singularity as well as to a pole.

Parametrize the positively oriented unit circle by z=eiθ. Then e−1/z=e−cosθ+isinθ and dz=ieiθdθ, so
∮C​e−1/zdz=i∫02π​e−cosθcos(θ+sinθ)dθ−∫02π​e−cosθsin(θ+sinθ)dθ.
(3)
Equating the real part and imaginary part with −2πi gives
∫02π​e−cosθcos(θ+sinθ)dθ=−2π,∫02π​e−cosθsin(θ+sinθ)dθ=0.​

Solution
Words: 53
a OurBigBook.com
The Joukowski map f(z)=z+z−1 is holomorphic on C∖{0}. A holomorphic function is locally conformal where its derivative is nonzero. Here f′(z)=1−z−2 vanishes at z=±1. Therefore
holomorphic on C∖{0};conformal at every point except 0,1,−1,​
(5)
where the exclusion of zero is because the function is undefined there. Holomorphy alone does not supply conformality at the two critical points.

b

Words: 58 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 58
b OurBigBook.com
Put z=1+ζ. Expanding the holomorphic function near its critical point gives
f(1+ζ)=2+ζ2−ζ3+O(ζ4).
(6)
For a small ray ζ=reiθ, the leading image displacement is r2e2iθ. Thus oriented ray angles are doubled modulo 2π at z=1. This is angle multiplication at a holomorphic critical point of multiplicity two; an unoriented angle between full tangent lines must also be interpreted modulo π. The map is not locally one-to-one there.

c

Words: 69 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 69
c OurBigBook.com
For z=eiθ the image is w=2cosθ, a real number. Therefore each semicircle maps onto the real interval [−2,2], with endpoints included for closed semicircles. Under positive traversal of the full unit circle, the upper half runs from 2 to −2 and the lower half returns from −2 to 2. Every interior point has two unit-circle preimages. The Joukowski circle-to-ellipse mapping degenerates to a doubled line segment at this radius.

d

Words: 73 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 73
d OurBigBook.com
For a radius ρ>0, write z=ρeiθ. Then
w=(ρ+ρ−1)cosθ+i(ρ−ρ−1)sinθ.
(7)
For ρ=1 its image is the ellipse
(ρ+ρ−1)2(Rew)2​+(ρ−ρ−1)2(Imw)2​=1.​
(8)
Its horizontal semiaxis is ρ+ρ−1, its vertical semiaxis is ∣ρ−ρ−1∣, and its foci are ±2 because the squared semiaxes differ by 4. Reciprocal radii give the same ellipse, traversed in opposite directions as θ increases.

a

Solution
Words: 70
a OurBigBook.com
The square-root branch points are zero and infinity. At zero the local behavior is z−1/2; in the coordinate u=1/z near infinity it is u1/2. In either case one circuit reverses the sign and two restore it. Thus the ramification index is 2: these are two-sheeted algebraic branch points, sometimes described as branch order one when order means ramification index minus one. The decay to zero at infinity does not remove the branching.

Solution
Words: 203
b OurBigBook.com
TODO: the original closed-contour drawing is absent from the source. The following independent Bromwich contour deformation establishes the required discontinuity relation without asserting the missing drawing's exact geometry. Orient the vertical line upward, as required by the positive imaginary answer in the next part, and use the principal square root, −π<argz<π.
Close a truncated vertical line to the left with a rectangle, slit it along the negative real axis, and exclude a small circle about zero. The integrand is holomorphic inside that slit domain, so the boundary contour integral is zero. Horizontal boundary integrals are O(R−1/2): integrating ex along −R≤x≤1 gives a bounded factor while ∣z∣−1/2≤R−1/2. The left boundary contributes O(e−RR1/2), and the small circle contributes O(ε​). All vanish in the indicated limits.
At z=−x with x>0, the upper and lower bank values are respectively −ie−x/x​ and +ie−x/x​. The boundary follows the upper bank toward zero and the lower bank away from zero. Their combined contribution is −2i∫0∞​e−xx−1/2dx. Hence
I=2i∫0∞​e−xx−1/2dx.​
(9)
The vertically improper integral converges conditionally; these estimates also justify the contour limit. Reversing the vertical orientation reverses its sign.

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
The Gamma function identity Γ(1/2)=π​ gives the Bromwich integral of an inverse square root directly:
I=2iΓ(1/2)=2iπ​.​
(10)
Equivalently, put x=u2 in the real integral. It becomes 2∫0∞​e−u2du=π​ by the Gaussian integral.

1 OurBigBook.com
For two bodies of masses M1​,M2​, the relative Kepler orbit has semimajor axis a and orbital period P satisfying Kepler's third law
P2=G(M1​+M2​)4π2a3​.​
(11)
Here a is the semimajor axis of the separation vector, not either star's individual barycentric orbit. In conventional stellar units the same relation is approximately (P/yr)2=(a/AU)3/[(M1​+M2​)/M⊙​], with year, astronomical unit and solar mass as the units.

2

Words: 68 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 68
2 OurBigBook.com
Equal radial velocity amplitudes imply equal stellar masses. Under the circular, edge-on eclipsing binary interpretation, each star moves at K=100kms−1, and the relative speed is 2K. Thus
a=2π(K1​+K2​)P​=1.499×1010m,M1​+M2​=2πGP(K1​+K2​)3​.
(12)
Using P=5.45 days gives
a≃0.100AU,M1​=M2​≃2.26M⊙​.​
(13)
More generally, spectroscopic binary amplitudes determine asini=P(K1​+K2​)1−e2​/(2π) and (M1​+M2​)sin3i=P(K1​+K2​)3(1−e2)3/2/(2πG). Thus these numerical masses and separation use e=0, sini=1; eclipses alone imply high inclination rather than its exact value.

Words: 146
3 OurBigBook.com
TODO: the source light curve, its numerical contact phases and the meanings of the four plotted time labels are absent, so unique numerical stellar radii cannot be recovered. The central eclipse contact-radius relations explain what the missing measurements would determine.
If t1​,…,t4​ denote the usual first through fourth contacts of a central eclipse, define T14​=t4​−t1​ and T23​=t3​−t2​, and let RL​≥RS​ be the two radii. For a circular edge-on orbit,
RL​+RS​=asinPπT14​​,RL​−RS​=asinPπT23​​.
(14)
Taking half their sum and difference gives the radii. For short eclipses the familiar approximation is RL​≃vrel​(T14​+T23​)/4 and RS​≃vrel​(T14​−T23​)/4, with vrel​=2K. At first and fourth contact the discs touch externally; at second and third the smaller disc is just internally tangent to the larger. Noncentral eclipses require the projected impact parameter as well.

Words: 105
1 OurBigBook.com
Build the star by adding spherical shells. With m(r) the enclosed mass, its gravitational binding energy is
Ω=−∫0M⊙​​r(m)Gm​dm.
(15)
For a nondegenerate extended star, r(m)<R⊙​ on the interior, so
∣Ω∣>R⊙​G​∫0M⊙​​mdm=2R⊙​GM⊙2​​.​
(16)
This is a gravitational binding-energy lower bound for a spherical star. The Kelvin-Helmholtz cooling time is of order
τKH​∼R⊙​L⊙​GM⊙2​​≃3.1×107yr.​
(17)
The displayed energy bound gives ∣Ω∣/L⊙​>1.6×107 years; it supplies a lower bound on that reservoir-to-luminosity ratio. A stellar structure model sets its coefficient. For an ideal monatomic, gas-supported star the virial theorem puts about half the released gravitational energy into heat, leaving half available for radiation; a uniform-density model would give about 9×106 years. These contraction estimates are all of order 107 years, much shorter than the nuclear lifetime.

Solution
Words: 74
2 OurBigBook.com
Use the supplied atomic masses consistently. Their mass defect per four hydrogen atoms is 4(1.0078)−4.0026=0.0286 atomic mass units. The conversion efficiency is
ϵ=4mH​4mH​−mHe​​=0.007095≃0.71%.​
(18)
The atomic-mass bookkeeping includes the associated positron-annihilation energy; an exact photon-heating budget also subtracts energy carried away by neutrinos. With the stated ten-percent fuel fraction and constant present solar luminosity, the main sequence lifetime estimate is
τMS​≃L⊙​0.1ϵM⊙​c2​≃1.05×1010yr.​
(19)
The much longer timescale explains why stellar nuclear fusion can power the Sun throughout its long main-sequence history.

3

Words: 137 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 137
3 OurBigBook.com
A Hertzsprung-Russell diagram plots stellar luminosity upward and effective temperature increasing toward the left. The main sequence runs from hot luminous stars at upper left to cool faint stars at lower right, with the Sun near Teff​≃5800K, L=L⊙​.
In the evolution of a solar-mass star, core hydrogen fusion initially supplies the luminosity. As core hydrogen is exhausted, hydrogen-shell fusion around a contracting helium core carries the star through the subgiant and red giant phases toward higher luminosity and lower surface temperature. Helium ignition is followed by core helium fusion with a hydrogen-burning shell, placing a solar-mass star in the red clump. The later Asymptotic giant branch has hydrogen- and helium-burning shells around a carbon-oxygen core. Envelope ejection exposes a hot central star of a planetary nebula; residual shell burning ends and the resulting white dwarf radiates stored thermal energy as it cools.

Thermal interstellar dust produces a bright galactic foreground concentrated toward the Milky Way plane, with additional cloud structure. Its emission spectrum differs from the approximately 2.73K blackbody spectrum of the cosmic microwave background, so comparisons across frequencies help separate it. In the sketch below this is the bright equatorial band.

Solution
Words: 44
b OurBigBook.com
Observer motion produces the cosmic microwave background dipole: to first order in β=v/c,
T0​ΔT(θ)​=βcosθ.
(20)
The direction of motion is hotter and the opposite direction cooler. Its full-sky pattern has one broad positive hemisphere and one broad negative hemisphere; it is not concentrated in the galactic plane.

c

Words: 61 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 61
c OurBigBook.com
After subtracting the mean, the motion-induced dipole and galactic foregrounds, intrinsic Cosmic microwave background anisotropy appears as angular hot and cold patches, typically at the 10−5 fractional scale. These spatial temperature fluctuations encode early density and velocity structure. The displayed patch pattern is illustrative, with no claim to reproduce an observed sky map.

Solution
Words: 84
1 OurBigBook.com
Measure the absolute spectral radiance over a range of frequencies and fit the Planck spectrum
Bν​(T)=c22hν3​ehν/(kB​T)−11​.
(21)
For example, the COBE FIRAS blackbody spectrum experiment used a differential Michelson interferometer to compare the sky with an internal blackbody; an external calibrated blackbody could cover the sky entrance. Cold bolometers measured the difference spectrum, and foreground separation distinguished Milky Way emission from the nearly isotropic background. The fitted background temperature is approximately T0​=2.73K​.[ref] The result relies on an absolute spectral comparison, rather than merely measuring a map's hot-to-cold contrast.

v=0.00105c≃3.15×105ms−1=315kms−1.​
(22)
The motion is toward the hotter region. The contrast already gives one side relative to the mean; the hot-to-cold difference would be twice as large.

Adiabatic expansion preserves the blackbody form while each photon's energy redshifts as a−1. Thus the cosmic microwave background temperature obeys T(z)=T0​(1+z), giving
T(z=3)=4T0​≃10.9K.​
(23)

Convert both inputs to energy density. The matter contribution, including rest energy, is uM,0​=ρM,0​c2=2.25×10−10Jm−3. The given photon value is uγ,0​=5×105(1.602×10−19)=8.01×10−14Jm−3. Hence
uγ,0​uM,0​​≃2.80×103.​
(24)
Matter energy density scales as (1+z)3, whereas the cosmic microwave background scales as (1+z)4. The photon-only matter-radiation equality condition is therefore
1+zeq​=uγ,0​uM,0​​,zeq​≃2.8×103.​
(25)
This uses the supplied CMB photon density. Additional relativistic species change equality for total radiation.

S3 (Quantum ideas)

Words: 2k Articles: 35
2012 OurBigBook.com

1

Words: 554 Articles: 8
S3 OurBigBook.com

1

Words: 146 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 146
1 OurBigBook.com
Black-body radiation and the photoelectric effect exposed failures of classical continuous-wave energy exchange. Classical equipartition predicted an unbounded short-wavelength thermal spectrum, the ultraviolet catastrophe. Quantized oscillator energies En​=nhν give the mean excitation energy hν/(ehν/(kB​T)−1) and suppress high-frequency modes, producing Planck's law. In the modern description, thermal radiation consists of photons with energy hν and Bose occupation numbers.
For the photoelectric effect, increasing intensity below a threshold frequency does not eject electrons, whereas the maximum electron kinetic energy grows with frequency above threshold. Absorption of one photon transfers hν to one electron, giving Kmax​=hν−W​ and threshold ν0​=W/h, where W is the work function. Intensity primarily changes the photon arrival rate and hence the photocurrent in the ordinary single-photon regime. Thus changing energy per quantum and changing the number of quanta have distinct consequences. Historically the thermal derivation first quantized matter's energy exchange; it should not be described as an already complete derivation of modern photon theory.

2

Words: 97 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 97
2 OurBigBook.com
For a photon, pγ​=E/c and λγ​=hc/E. The neutron is nonrelativistic here because 18.8keV≪mn​c2, so pn​=2mn​E​ and λn​=h/pn​. Using the supplied common energy gives
pγ​=1.005×10−23kgms−1,λγ​=6.595×10−11m,​
(26)
pn​=3.176×10−21kgms−1,λn​=2.086×10−13m.​
(27)
Equal kinetic energies do not imply equal momenta: the massive particle obeys E=p2/(2mn​), while the massless photon obeys E=pc. The neutron momentum is about 316 times larger, so its de Broglie wavelength is about 316 times smaller.
To give the neutron the photon wavelength, set its momentum to E/c, not its kinetic energy to E again. Then
vn​≃mn​cE​=5.999×103ms−1.​
(28)

In the Franck-Hertz experiment, electrons emitted from a heated cathode are accelerated through a dilute atomic vapour toward a collector. A small retarding potential before the collector rejects electrons that have lost too much kinetic energy. Below the first excitation threshold, mainly elastic collisions occur and the collector current rises as the accelerating voltage increases. At threshold an inelastic collision can transfer a definite excitation energy to an atom, causing a current drop because the slowed electron cannot overcome the retarding potential.
Raising the voltage further permits acceleration again, and repeated losses produce successive current minima. For mercury their spacing is about 4.9V, corresponding to an atomic excitation of about 4.9eV and an associated ultraviolet photon near 254nm. Contact potentials shift the absolute voltages, so the spacing is more informative than the first minimum's position alone. Discrete energy losses support discrete atomic energy levels; a continuously variable excitation energy would not produce the same recurring fixed loss scale. The experiment establishes quantized excitations without requiring the classical electron orbit of the Bohr model to be literally correct.

A classical orbiting electron accelerates and therefore radiates according to the Larmor formula. Its mechanical energy becomes more negative, its radius decreases, and the orbit spirals inward rather than remaining a stable atom. The Bohr model replaces this prediction with postulated nonradiating stationary states and quantized orbital angular momentum, together with photon emission or absorption only between states, hν=∣En​−Em​∣.
For a heavy nucleus, me​vr=nℏ. Since the de Broglie wavelength is h/(me​v), this implies
2πr=nλ,n=1,2,….​
(34)
The electronic wave fits an integer number of wavelengths around the orbit. This is a standing-wave consistency interpretation of the quantization rule, not a classical mechanism that prevents an accelerating charge from radiating. For finite nuclear mass, the two-body relative coordinate uses reduced mass μ=me​M/(me​+M); the next derivation retains that correction. In the limit M≫me​, it reduces to the fixed-nucleus electron description above.

The differential term is the kinetic energy operator acting on the wave function, V(x) supplies the multiplicative potential energy, and their sum is the Hamiltonian operator. The eigenvalue E is the stationary state's total energy. This form assumes a nonrelativistic particle, a time-independent scalar potential, and no additional internal degrees of freedom in the stated model.

⟨x⟩=∫x∣ψ(x)∣2dx,⟨x2⟩=∫x2∣ψ(x)∣2dx.​
(43)
The integrals run over the allowed domain. If the given state is not normalized, divide both by ∫∣ψ∣2dx. Its variance is ⟨x2⟩−⟨x⟩2; neither ψ itself nor its overall phase is a directly measured position probability.

∣ψ(t)⟩=2​e−iE1​t/ℏ∣1⟩+e−iE2​t/ℏ∣2⟩​.
(44)
Orthonormality removes all off-diagonal terms from the expected value of the energy, giving
⟨E⟩=2E1​+E2​​,independent of time.​

Return up to an overall phase requires the relative phase to return to one. For E1​=E2​, the shortest positive recurrence time is
τ=∣E2​−E1​∣2πℏ​.​

If the two energies coincide, the whole superposition is stationary up to a common phase for every time; there is then no smallest strictly positive recurrence time. A half-period changes the relative sign and produces the orthogonal antisymmetric state rather than the original symmetric state.

Annual conversion is reduced by several multiplicative losses. Only roughly 40–50% of incident sunlight lies in the photosynthetically useful visible band. Reflection and transmission prevent complete absorption; the photon budget and unavoidable relaxation losses limit conversion of absorbed radiation into chemical energy. Photosynthesis also has to support respiration and maintenance, while seasonal growth, incomplete canopy cover, water and nutrient limitations reduce the annual harvested yield.
An illustrative loss budget, not a universal biological constant, is 0.45×0.8×0.25×0.5×0.11≃0.005. The factors represent useful spectrum, absorption, photochemical conversion, retained net production, and combined annual interception and growing-condition limitations, respectively. Thus ηannual​∼0.5%​ is plausible for a land-averaged crop yield even though a leaf under favourable illumination can be more efficient. The result depends on crop, climate, harvested fraction and the definition of dry biomass energy. When the input is already annual mean insolation, night-time must not be counted as a second independent loss.

Three advantages of biomass energy are:
  • Sustainable regrowth can replenish the fuel and recycle its biogenic carbon, unlike depletion of fossil carbon stocks.
  • Chemical fuel can be stored and transported, permitting dispatchable heat, electricity or liquid-fuel production rather than requiring use at the instant of sunlight capture.
  • Suitable agricultural residues and organic wastes can supply useful energy while recovering value from material that would otherwise need disposal.
Three disadvantages are:
  • Dedicated energy crops compete for land and water, potentially displacing food production and damaging biodiversity.
  • Low annual areal productivity, bulky feedstock and moisture increase collection, transport, drying and conversion costs.
  • Combustion produces local air pollutants, and processing emissions or land-use carbon debt can undermine the claimed climate saving. A life-cycle assessment and a regrowth timescale are necessary; “renewable” alone does not prove low net emissions.

An ideal Rankine cycle has four main steps: liquid water is pumped reversibly to high pressure; heat is added at high pressure to produce hot vapour or supercritical working fluid; the fluid expands approximately isentropically through a turbine to produce work; and low-pressure heat rejection in a condenser returns it to liquid. For steady flow, the main work and heat transfers are differences of specific enthalpy.
A steam implementation of the Carnot cycle would require compression of a wet liquid-vapour mixture and reversible isothermal heat transfer, both difficult to achieve with practical machinery. Complete condensation before the Rankine pump makes compression work small because liquid specific volume is small. High-pressure heating and superheating can then occur in a boiler without demanding isothermal addition of all the heat. Superheating also reduces turbine-exit moisture, although the calculated exit may still be wet. The pump, turbine, condenser and boiler can operate continuously as separate flow devices. The Rankine cycle sacrifices some ideal thermal efficiency in return for a practicable steam-plant configuration; no real engine can exceed the Carnot efficiency for the same extreme reservoir temperatures.

Post-combustion carbon capture and storage separates carbon dioxide from an already formed flue gas, often by absorption in a regenerable solvent. The recovered gas must be purified, dehydrated, compressed, transported and injected into a suitable geological store. Caprock integrity, trapping mechanisms, monitoring and long-term liability matter as much as capture at the chimney.
Dilute carbon dioxide mixed with nitrogen requires a large gas-processing plant. Solvent regeneration consumes heat; compression consumes power; impurities can cause solvent degradation and corrosion. Retrofitting adds equipment, cooling demand and cost, and lowers net electrical output per unit fuel. Storage capacity, injection performance, leakage risk and public acceptance must be demonstrated, while upstream fuel-cycle emissions remain.
A capture fraction is not the same as the reduction per delivered kilowatt-hour. For illustrative capture χ=0.9 and a plant-efficiency decrease from 0.4 to 0.3, residual stack emissions per delivered unit scale as (1−χ)(0.4/0.3)=0.133, corresponding to an 86.7% reduction rather than 90%. A full life-cycle assessment includes the additional fuel and upstream emissions. These figures illustrate the accounting and are not claimed as universal plant performance.

Variability reduces firm capacity and creates balancing costs, but does not impose a universal tiny upper limit on the energy fraction from wind power. As an illustrative scale calculation, 10GW installed at capacity factor 0.30 produces 26.3TWh annually, about 8.8% of an assumed 300TWh annual demand. Larger installations can supply larger fractions if the rest of the system is adapted.
Geographical spread, forecasting, interconnection, flexible generation, demand response and energy storage manage fluctuations on different timescales. They are not interchangeable: a battery that balances seconds does not necessarily cover a week of low wind. Correlated weather, curtailment, network constraints and reserve requirements become more important at high penetration. Backup capacity need not burn fuel continuously at the wind plant's nameplate output; energy and capacity should be accounted for separately. The defensible conclusion is that significant penetration requires system planning and has costs, not that variability alone confines wind to a negligible contribution.[ref]

The judgement depends on the objectives and the replacement system, rather than following from a single technological fact. In the 2012 context, Germany had decided after Fukushima to accelerate its planned nuclear exit, with a timetable then extending to 2022. The contemporary official statement presented this as a reassessment of residual risk and a transition to efficiency and renewable supply.[ref]
There is a serious climate opportunity cost if low-operational-carbon nuclear generation is replaced by unabated fossil generation. For example, replacing an illustrative 100TWhyear−1 with generation emitting 400 or 900gCO2​kWh−1 adds 40 or 90 million tonnes of carbon dioxide annually. Replacing that energy by wind at capacity factor 0.30 would require about 38GW of nameplate capacity, plus an adequate reliability plan; equal annual energy is not equal firm capacity.
Against continued operation must be weighed accident consequences, waste management, ageing, public preferences and the costs and feasibility of alternatives. Germany's specific risk assessment cannot be inferred solely from the different geography of Fukushima. A fast exit without credible low-carbon replacement can conflict with emissions goals; an exit supported by efficiency, infrastructure and low-carbon alternatives can pursue other legitimate objectives. Calling the decision intrinsically rational or irrational without those comparisons is not a technical conclusion. This answer evaluates the choice as posed in 2012, rather than importing later events as foreknowledge.

Tidal power offers predictable astronomical timing, while wave power can exploit an energetic marine resource. Neither is constant: tidal streams have slack-water periods, and wave energy varies with weather and season. Diversity can help a renewable portfolio, but resource size does not by itself establish economical extractable output.
For scale, a mean marine output of 5GW would produce 43.8TWh per year, about 15% of an assumed 300TWh annual electricity demand. Achieving that mean at capacity factor 0.30 would require about 17GW installed. This is an illustrative deployment requirement, not a measured UK resource estimate or a 2012 forecast. Tidal-stream kinetic power density scales as ρv3/2, making energetic sites valuable, but channel-wide extraction also changes the flow, so isolated-rotor power densities cannot simply be multiplied by sea area.
Harsh marine conditions, access for maintenance, survivability in storms, cable connections, navigation and ecological effects constrain deployment. Barrages additionally change estuaries and sediment transport. Research and demonstration may be worthwhile for energy diversity and industrial capability, but “important to investigate” is weaker than “indispensable at any cost”. Marine investment should be compared with efficiency and other low-carbon options using delivered energy, system value and environmental impacts.

The MENA solar resource could provide a useful supplement, but geographical potential does not make imports logically essential to European decarbonisation. With an illustrative annual mean insolation 200Wm−2, photovoltaic conversion 15% and system factor 0.8, mean delivered-at-plant power is 24Wm−2. A collector area of 104km2 would then give 240GW mean or about 2100TWh annually before export losses. This is a scale calculation with stipulated assumptions, not a land-availability survey.
Long transmission corridors, converter losses, night-time supply, storage, dust, cooling or cleaning water, financing and political dependence must also be included. Solar thermal storage can shift some output but does not remove every seasonal or geopolitical risk. Projects should benefit host populations and avoid treating nominal desert area as empty infrastructure-ready land.
Europe also has domestic wind power, solar power, hydroelectricity, potential nuclear generation, demand reduction and other mitigation options. A technically credible combination of those is a counterexample to the word “essential”. MENA imports could reduce costs or improve diversity within a broader low-carbon system; whether they are preferable requires a complete system comparison rather than solar resource density alone.

A common minimum carbon price can make the external cost of emissions visible in investment and dispatch decisions, encourage reductions where they are cheapest, and reduce incentives to relocate emissions-intensive production to unpriced jurisdictions. A credible rising or durable price signal can be more useful for long-lived investment than a volatile short-term spot price.
For an illustrative price of 40 currency units per tonne of carbon dioxide, generation emitting 0.9 tonnes per MWh incurs 36 units per MWh, while generation at 0.4 tonnes per MWh incurs 16. Those changes are large enough to affect some operating choices, but the actual switching point depends on fuel prices, efficiency and capacity constraints.
A price is not sufficient by itself. Measurement, enforcement, distributional effects and revenue use matter; infrastructure, innovation spillovers, information failures and landlord-tenant incentives can justify complementary policies. Nor is a uniform international minimum a logical prerequisite for any effective reduction: standards, clean-power deployment and efficiency policies can reduce emissions even before every country agrees. The strongest defensible claim is that broad, credible pricing is a valuable coordination instrument, not a uniquely necessary or automatically sufficient solution.[ref]

A plug-in hybrid electric vehicle can move short journeys to electricity while retaining liquid-fuel range for longer ones. It can reduce oil dependence and some local tailpipe emissions, but the carbon benefit depends on charging, trip length, electricity supply, vehicle manufacture and the fuel used when the engine runs.
For illustration, electricity consumption 0.20kWhkm−1 at grid intensity 500gCO2​kWh−1 gives 100gCO2​km−1 in use. A petrol vehicle using 0.07 litres per km emits about 158gCO2​km−1 from combustion under the paper's octane-density assumptions. Ignoring other life-cycle differences, their use-phase break-even electricity intensity is therefore roughly 790gCO2​kWh−1. Cleaner electricity improves the electric case; sufficiently carbon-intensive electricity can reverse it. These are conditional comparisons, not measured fleet averages.
A plug-in hybrid that is rarely charged may obtain little benefit while carrying both propulsion systems. Battery and fuel production also belong in a life-cycle assessment. Fully electric vehicles, efficient conventional vehicles, public transport, walking, cycling and reduced travel demand provide alternative or complementary routes. Plug-in hybrids can be a useful transition technology, but no physical argument makes them an essential component of every successful climate strategy.

Stylized facts of financial returns are robust qualitative statistical regularities found across many instruments or datasets, abstracting from their individual details. Examples include heavy return-distribution tails relative to a Gaussian model, weak linear autocorrelation of many liquid-market returns beyond short lags, and persistent clustering of large absolute or squared returns. Some markets also show asymmetric return-volatility responses and partial movement toward a Gaussian aggregate distribution at longer horizons.
These are empirical tendencies with sampling-scale and market qualifications, not exact universal equations. In particular, weak return autocorrelation does not imply independent increments: volatility clustering and higher-order dependence can remain. A useful model should state which regularities it explains and which its assumptions exclude, rather than treating one convenient random-walk model as an observed law.

Let ST​ be the terminal asset price and K a common strike or forward delivery price. A long European call and put have expiry payoffs
CT​=(ST​−K)+,PT​=(K−ST​)+.​
(89)
The call is zero below K and then rises with slope one; the put falls with slope minus one below K and is zero above it. A long forward instead has FTlong​=ST​−K​ and a short forward has FTshort​=K−ST​​. Both are straight lines crossing zero at K, with negative as well as positive outcomes.
The option's exercise right truncates the unfavourable side, whereas the forward is an obligation. These are payoffs, not total profits: an option premium and its financing cost have not been subtracted. A newly agreed fair forward may have zero initial value while still having a nonzero future delivery price.

Assume a non-dividend-paying tradable asset follows geometric Brownian motion dS=μSdt+σSdW, with constant volatility σ and risk-free rate r. Trading is continuous, frictionless and divisible; borrowing and lending occur at the same rate, short selling is allowed, the strategy is self-financing, and there are no jumps or arbitrage opportunities. These are modelling assumptions, not assertions that market returns are exactly Gaussian or that hedging is costless in practice.
For a smooth option price V(S,t), Itô's formula gives
dV=(Vt​+μSVS​+21​σ2S2VSS​)dt+σSVS​dW.
(90)
Replicate it by Δ shares and a cash account of value b=V−ΔS. Self-financing requires dV=ΔdS+rbdt. Matching the stochastic term fixes Δ=VS​. Matching the remaining drift and cancelling the physical drift μ then gives
Vt​+21​σ2S2VSS​+rSVS​−rV=0.​
(91)
This is the Black-Scholes equation. The cancellation does not assert that the actual expected asset return equals r; risk-neutral valuation is a consequence of replication under these assumptions.
For a European call, impose V(S,T)=(S−K)+, with V(0,t)=0 and V(S,t)∼S−Ke−r(T−t) for large S. Its writer hedges the short option by holding Δ=∂V/∂S shares and investing or borrowing the residual cash V−ΔS, rebalancing as S and time change. In the constant-parameter model Δ=N(d1​), where d1​=[log(S/K)+(r+σ2/2)(T−t)]/[σT−t​] and N is the standard normal cumulative distribution. Continuous rebalancing is an ideal limit: transaction costs, discrete trading, jumps and changing volatility create residual hedge risk. Writing the self-financing gains equation explicitly avoids incorrectly adding an unfinanced SdΔ term to the strategy.

Implied volatility is the volatility parameter that makes a specified option-pricing model reproduce an observed option price. For a call, it solves
CBS​(S,K,T−t,r;σimp​)=Cmarket​.​

For positive time to expiry and positive asset and strike prices, the Black-Scholes call price increases with σ, so an interior arbitrage-consistent price gives a unique finite positive value. It is an inverse model parameter, not the sample standard deviation of past returns or a guaranteed forecast of future realised volatility. Different implied volatilities across strikes or maturities form smiles or surfaces, signalling that one constant volatility does not fit all prices simultaneously.

Independent identically distributed increments have the same marginal distribution at every step and factorizing joint distributions across steps. With finite mean μ and variance s2, an additive random walk has mean displacement nμ and variance ns2 after n steps. Zero increment autocovariances follow from independence, but their converse is false. Gaussian increments are an additional assumption, not part of the definition of a random walk.
To investigate a measured price process, first specify the sampling interval and whether the model concerns price differences or log returns. Remove an estimated drift and examine stationarity, increment distributions, autocorrelations and variance growth over nonoverlapping horizons. Also test higher-order statistics, absolute or squared-return correlations, conditional distributions and out-of-sample predictability; those can reveal dependence missed by linear autocorrelation. Check whether different time scales and market regimes give compatible results, and account for bid-ask effects and intraday seasonality at short lags. Finite data cannot prove independence or permanent stationarity. Failure to reject a particular test is weaker than establishing that every joint distribution factorizes; the next example makes that distinction explicit.

For example, the observed past feature Zt​=Xt−1​Xt−2​ satisfies E[Xt​Zt​]=1 and EZt2​=4, so its least-squares predictor within the family bZt​ is Xt​=Zt​/4​. A finite bound on ordinary peak-to-trough financial drawdown does not follow. Choose a long alternating sequence of driving signs, at​=(−1)t. It produces Xt​=−1+(−1)t, alternating −2 and 0. The price never recovers during that episode and its cumulative loss grows without bound as the episode length grows. Every finite such driving sequence has positive probability. Thus no finite worst drawdown magnitude or duration exists without a horizon bound.​
More precisely, over an N-month window and over admissible starting histories, the maximum possible drawdown is
Dmax​(N)=2⌊N/2⌋+2(N≥1).​
(96)
One derivation keeps the last two signs as a four-state dynamic program. Let dn​(a,b) be the smallest cumulative increment after n steps ending with signs (a,b), with d0​(a,b)=0 for each permitted initial pair. Then dn+1​(b,c)=mina=±1​[dn​(a,b)+ab+c]. Induction gives the negative of the displayed minimum. The bound is attained by increments (−2,0)k,−2 for N=2k+1, or (−2,0)k−1,−2,−2 for N=2k, so it is also an attained peak-to-trough loss over N months, not only an algebraic net displacement bound.
For comparison, the index with increments at​=±1 has Dmax​(N)=N, attained by N successive negative signs; it too has no finite horizon-free bound. If “drawdown” were intended to mean a strictly decreasing consecutive run, the first model permits at most two successive −2 increments, for a loss of four over two months, whereas the simple walk permits arbitrarily long such runs. That different run statistic must not be substituted for the usual drawdown definition: zero increments can separate continuing losses without any recovery.

Derivatives can transfer risk, improve price discovery and permit hedging, so their existence is not by itself evidence that they cause crashes. They can also amplify stress through leverage, margin calls, counterparty exposure and forced dynamic hedging into falling markets. A short-gamma hedge can require selling more underlying after a fall, reinforcing feedback when liquidity is thin. The causal issue is the combination of positions, funding, market depth and institutional rules; derivatives are neither necessary nor sufficient for a crash, and correlation between trading volume and a crash does not establish the direction of causation.

Financial data show approximate, scale-dependent regularities rather than an exact universal scaling law. Heavy return tails can resemble a power law over an intermediate range, but the fitted exponent, cutoff and range depend on instrument, period and sampling. A straight segment on a log-log plot alone is not enough to establish a power law.
For independent finite-variance increments, variance grows linearly with horizon and typical fluctuations scale as Δt1/2. Central-limit aggregation can make longer-horizon returns more Gaussian even when short-horizon returns are heavy-tailed. Real data can depart from a single self-similar distribution because of volatility clustering, changing regimes, asymmetric responses, intraday seasonality and market microstructure. Apparent different scaling of higher moments may reflect intermittent volatility, but moments estimated from rare tails can also be unstable or may not exist in an idealized model.
Useful tests compare rescaled distributions, structure functions and volatility correlations across several scales, with uncertainty estimates and checks for nonstationarity. Scaling is a valuable approximate modelling guide over a documented range, not proof that one exponent describes every asset and horizon or that historical tail behaviour fixes future extreme losses.

Protein primary structure is the ordered amino acid sequence of a polypeptide, linked by covalent peptide bonds. The approximately planar peptide bond restricts local geometry, while backbone torsion angles give conformational freedom subject to steric exclusion. Protein secondary structure comprises local backbone arrangements, especially the alpha helix, with backbone hydrogen bonds between residues i and i+4, and the beta sheet, whose strands are joined by backbone hydrogen bonds. Turns and loops connect these elements. Protein tertiary structure is the full three-dimensional organization of a single chain, often including several protein domains. Protein quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple chains in a protein complex.
Protein folding is governed by the Gibbs free energy of the chain together with its solvent, not by the chain's energy alone. Folding reduces the chain's conformational entropy, but can gain solvent entropy through the hydrophobic effect, burying nonpolar side chains away from water. Favorable hydrogen bonds, Van der Waals forces, electrostatic interactions and sometimes covalent disulfide bonds stabilize particular structures. Steric repulsion prevents atomic overlap. At fixed temperature and pressure, the native ensemble is favored when its total ΔG=ΔH−TΔS is lower than competing ensembles. The balance depends on the solvent, pH, salt and ligands. Molecular chaperones help avoid aggregation or kinetic traps; a stable fold is not a perfectly rigid conformation, and some proteins have disordered regions.
For a soluble globular protein, a typical pattern is a nonpolar core and a polar, hydrated surface. A transmembrane protein instead presents nonpolar side chains to the hydrocarbon interior of the lipid bilayer. Membrane-spanning alpha helices satisfy their polar backbone groups through internal hydrogen bonds; a roughly membrane-thickness helix commonly contains about twenty residues, depending on tilt and bilayer thickness. Multiple helices can enclose polar channels or binding sites. Membrane-spanning beta barrels likewise expose mainly nonpolar groups outward towards lipid while arranging backbone hydrogen bonds between strands and often lining an aqueous pore with polar groups. Exposed loops and domains contacting water can resemble soluble proteins. Not every membrane-associated protein spans the membrane: peripheral attachment and lipid anchoring are distinct possibilities.
The organizing distinction is the environment of each surface: water favors accessible polar groups, while the membrane core favors outward-facing nonpolar groups. Buried polar groups can still be essential to a transport pathway or catalytic site.

ATP synthase couples downhill proton motion across a cell membrane to synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. Its membrane-embedded Fo​ sector contains an a subunit with offset proton-access half-channels and a rotating c-subunit ring. Reversible protonation of sites on the ring permits rotation relative to the stationary a subunit. The central rotor transmits this motion through the γ shaft to the soluble F1​ head. A peripheral stator holds the head relative to the membrane sector. The common bacterial schematic has an α3​β3​ head, catalytic sites mainly on the three β subunits, and a central γ/ϵ rotor; accessory stator components depend on the organism.
The binding-change mechanism cycles the catalytic sites between open, loose-binding and tight-binding conformations. Rotor orientation changes their affinities for ADP, phosphate and ATP; the sites operate out of phase. Tight binding favors formation of bound ATP, and mechanical rotation changes the conformation to permit product release. In the ideal tightly coupled cycle, one revolution gives three catalytic turnovers:
3 ATP per 360∘,1 ATP per 120∘.​
(105)
The proton count is not universally fixed: an ideal ring with nc​ proton-carrying subunits gives nc​ protons per revolution and nc​/3 protons per synthesized ATP, before additional transport costs.
For a proton moving from side 1 to side 2, its molar electrochemical potential change is
ΔμH+​=RTlogaH+,1​aH+,2​​+F(ψ2​−ψ1​).
(106)
The chemical gradient and membrane electric potential difference together supply the proton-motive force. Synthesis requires the proton free-energy release to meet the positive Gibbs free energy of ATP synthesis. The coupling is reversible: isolated F1​ supplied with ATP can hydrolyse it and rotate its shaft, while the intact enzyme can use hydrolysis-driven rotation to pump protons against their gradient. The sketch is structural and schematic; it does not reconstruct the absent stepping trace.

Let S1​(t) be the probability that an ATP-waiting state has not yet bound a substrate molecule. A constant bimolecular binding coefficient k1​ at fixed ATP concentration c gives a pseudo-first-order hazard λ=k1​c. Thus S˙1​=−λS1​, S1​(0)=1, and the waiting-time distribution is
P1​(t)=−S˙1​(t)=k1​ce−k1​ct,t≥0,⟨t1​⟩=k1​c1​.​
(107)
The probability density function starts at k1​c and decreases exponentially. Increasing c shortens the waiting time in inverse proportion. This supports one rate-limiting ATP-binding event before the associated motion, rather than a concentration-independent chemical delay.
For the second delay, consider sequential independent first-order transitions A⟶ka​B⟶kb​C. Their dwell times have exponential distributions. The total waiting time is their sum, so convolution gives
P2​(t)=∫0t​ka​e−ka​skb​e−kb​(t−s)ds=ka​−kb​ka​kb​​(e−kb​t−e−ka​t),t≥0.​
(108)
It is normalized, symmetric under exchange of ka​,kb​, and has
⟨t2​⟩=ka​1​+kb​1​,Var(t2​)=ka2​1​+kb2​1​.​
(109)
Unlike one exponential delay, it vanishes at t=0, rises initially as ka​kb​t, reaches a maximum at tmode​=log(ka​/kb​)/(ka​−kb​) and eventually decays at the slower rate. For equal rates the continuous limit is P2​(t)=k2te−kt, an Erlang distribution with mode 1/k. If one rate is much faster than the other, the observed long-time behavior approaches one exponential. The sketch in the preceding section displays these shapes using arbitrary specified rates.
The simplest catalytic cycle compatible with the fits therefore contains an ATP-dependent binding delay and at least two resolvable ATP-concentration-independent kinetic events. Hydrolysis, product release and conformational changes are possible microscopic assignments, but the two-rate fit alone does not uniquely identify them or the order of ka​ and kb​. If each complete 120∘ cycle contains these three waits and step durations are negligible, its mean duration is (k1​c)−1+ka−1​+kb−1​ and the mean revolution rate is the inverse of three times this duration. Multiple catalytic sites can cooperate during that cycle.

Write the one-dimensional random walk endpoint as xm​=∑j=1m​ξj​, starting at the origin. Assume unbiased, independent increments, each with ⟨ξj​⟩=0 and ⟨ξj2​⟩=Δ. Expanding the square gives
⟨xm2​⟩=∑j​⟨ξj2​⟩+2∑i<j​⟨ξi​ξj​⟩.
(110)
Independence makes each cross expectation ⟨ξi​⟩⟨ξj​⟩=0. Consequently
⟨xm​⟩=0,⟨xm2​⟩=mΔ.​
(111)
Uncorrelated increments with the same second moments would suffice. Unbiasedness alone does not remove correlations: persistent or anticorrelated steps need not satisfy this result. The symbol Δ is already the mean-square step size, with units of length squared.

Let C(x) be the particle number density, U(x) the conservative potential energy and F=−dU/dx the applied force. In the overdamped regime a viscous drag coefficient ζ gives drift velocity vd​=F/ζ. Combining this drift with Fick's first law gives the number flux
J=−DdxdC​+ζF​C.
(112)
At thermal equilibrium, the Boltzmann distribution is Ceq​∝e−U/(kB​T), so dCeq​/dx=FCeq​/(kB​T). Setting its net flux to zero yields
0=FCeq​(ζ1​−kB​TD​),D=ζkB​T​=μkB​T,μ=ζ−1.​
(113)
This is the Einstein diffusion relation. The derivation assumes a dilute equilibrium suspension, uniform temperature, linear drift response and a well-defined long-time diffusion coefficient. With a nonzero conservative force, the full transport equation includes drift; the force-free equation in the next section describes spreading without that drift.

For constant D and no drift, particle conservation and Fick's first law give the one-dimensional diffusion equation ∂t​C=D∂x2​C. For C=At−1/2e−x2/(4Dt),
∂t​C=C(−2t1​+4Dt2x2​),∂x2​C=C(−2Dt1​+4D2t2x2​),
(114)
so direct substitution verifies the equation for t>0. The Gaussian integral fixes the normalization:
∫−∞∞​Cdx=A4πD​=N,C(x,t)=4πDt​N​exp(−4Dtx2​).​
(115)
This is the heat kernel for a point release, with C(x,0)=Nδ(x) in the distributional limit. It remains centered at zero while its width grows as t1/2 and its peak falls as t−1/2. To compute the second moment, set y=x/4Dt​:
⟨x2⟩=N1​∫x2Cdx=π​4Dt​∫−∞∞​y2e−y2dy=2Dt​,
(116)
using ∫y2e−y2dy=π​/2 over the whole real line, obtained by integration by parts.
If the mean number of independent unbiased jumps in time t is ⟨m⟩=ft, conditioning on m gives ⟨x2(t)⟩=Δ⟨m⟩=fΔt. Matching it to the continuum diffusion result yields
D=2fΔ​.​
(117)
For fixed-magnitude steps a, Δ=a2. The equality of second moments also holds for Poisson jump times independent of the increments; a Gaussian continuum approximation additionally requires many steps and finite step variance.

Landau damping is the collisionless decay of a plasma wave through resonant energy exchange with particles whose velocity is close to the wave's phase velocity vϕ​=ω/k. Particles slightly slower than the wave tend to gain energy from it; particles slightly faster can give energy to it. For the decreasing resonant part of a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, the net transfer is from the wave to the electrons, so the wave amplitude decays.
In the linear Vlasov equation description this is collisionless phase mixing, not a requirement for frequent particle collisions. Fine-scale structure develops in the velocity dependence of the perturbation even while the macroscopic electric field decreases. The resonant contribution to the growth rate has the sign of ∂f/∂v at a positive wave phase velocity: a negative slope produces damping, whereas a sufficiently positive slope can drive an instability. A population comparison must be local to the resonance; merely counting all particles faster and slower than the wave is not the criterion.

Define the one-dimensional thermal widths σp​=kB​Tp​/me​​ and σb​=kB​Tb​/me​​. Normalize each velocity distribution to its electron number density:
fp​(v)=2π​σp​np​​e−v2/(2σp2​),fb​(v)=2π​σb​nb​​e−(v−V)2/(2σb2​).
(118)
The total is f=fp​+fb​. It consists of a broad peak centred at zero and a much narrower displaced beam near V, with V≫σp​≫σb​. Their areas, rather than their peak heights, are np​ and nb​. A weak narrow beam can make a positive-slope region on its low-velocity side even while contributing little to the total density.

This is the region where beam drive can most readily overcome the negative plasma slope when that background changes little over the narrow beam width. It is an estimate for the first resonant unstable wave, not a proof that every beam-plasma dispersion relation has its exact marginal phase velocity at this value. np​nb​​≥e​σp3​v∗​σb2​​e−v∗2​/(2σp2​).

np​nb​​>CkB​Tp​me​​​Tp​VTb​​exp(−2kB​Tp​me​V2​),C=e​.​

Choose the zero of internal energy as a separated proton and electron, so the atom has energy −R. Its single-particle partition function contains eR/(kB​T):
Zsp,e​=ge​V(h22πme​kB​T​)3/2,Zsp,p​=gp​V(h22πmp​kB​T​)3/2,

(i∂+m)(i∂−m)ψ=[−γμγν∂μ​∂ν​−m2]ψ=0.

The ordinary derivatives commute, so only the symmetric part of γμγν contributes. Requiring this operator to factor the Klein-Gordon equation, (∂μ∂μ​+m2)ψ=0, for arbitrary free momenta gives
{γμ,γν}=2ημνI,{γμ​,γν​}=2ημν​I.​
(142)
Thus the Dirac matrices represent the corresponding Clifford algebra. The inference uses factorization for the general free equation; the fact that one specially chosen wavefunction happens to solve both equations would not alone determine every matrix anticommutator.

∂t​(ψ†ψ)=−∇⋅(ψ†σψ).
(156)
Thus with ρ=ψ†ψ and J=ψ†σψ, the lower-index four-current jμ​=(ρ,−J) obeys ∂μjμ​=0​.
For K=σ⋅p,
[K,H]=[K,V]=−iσ⋅∇V.
(157)
Consequently K is conserved for spatially constant V; a spatially uniform time-dependent scalar offset would also commute with it. For general nonuniform V it is not conserved. At nonzero momentum, (σ⋅p^​)2=I, so the helicity eigenvalues are +1,−1​. In the chosen constant-potential Weyl Hamiltonian, the positive E−V branch has helicity +1; the negative branch has −1. An expectation value in a superposition need not itself be an eigenvalue.

Evaluate the envelopes at their displayed arguments and set a=η∗ρ. The common phase e−iV0​t cancels from every bilinear. Direct use of the Pauli matrices gives
jμ​=(∣η∣2+∣ρ∣2,−2Rea,−2Ima,∣ρ∣2−∣η∣2).​

The physical longitudinal current is Jz​=∣η∣2−∣ρ∣2: the two density profiles move in opposite directions. Their separate transport identities give ∂t​(∣η∣2+∣ρ∣2)+∂z​(∣η∣2−∣ρ∣2)=0.
For a coherent superposition, the transverse currents Jx​=2Re(η∗ρ) and Jy​=2Im(η∗ρ) generally do not vanish. They are independent of x,y, so they contribute no divergence in this one-dimensional construction. Omitting them would give an incorrect local four-current. Pointwise, ∣J∣2=(∣η∣2+∣ρ∣2)2, so the pure two-component Weyl current is future null wherever the density is nonzero. If only one envelope is present, the current points entirely along its propagation direction; an incoherent average can remove the transverse interference terms.

Relativistic radiation is concentrated into an angle of order 1/γ around the instantaneous velocity. The emission direction sweeps past a tangent observer over an orbital interval of order ρ/(γc). Since the charge moves toward the observer, arrival times are compressed by an additional factor of order 1/γ2, giving the spectral scale ω∼cγ3/ρ.
The conventional numerical factor follows from the radiation Fourier phase. Near the tangent direction, circular motion gives
ω(t−cn^⋅r(t)​)≃ω(2γ2t​+6ρ2c2t3​).
(171)
With u=cγt/ρ, this becomes [ωρ/(2cγ3)](u+u3/3). The resulting Airy-type integrals are expressible through modified Bessel functions with tangent-plane argument ξ=ωρ/(3cγ3). The standard angle-integrated synchrotron radiation spectrum has shape
F(x)=x∫x∞​K5/3​(z)dz,x=ωc​ω​,ξ=2x​.
(172)
It therefore identifies
ωc​=2ρ3cγ3​,ϵc​=ℏωc​=23​ρℏc​γ3.​
(173)
The beaming argument supplies the physical scaling; the spectral integral fixes the conventional factor 3/2. Critical energy is a broad spectral scale, not a hard photon-energy cutoff.[ref]

Solution

ii OurBigBook.com
Particles are lost when a process drives their transverse amplitude or energy outside the machine's accepted region. Principal causes include scattering from residual gas; Touschek scattering within a bunch, which can convert transverse momentum into excessive longitudinal momentum; collision losses at an interaction point; diffusion from nonlinear resonances, field or RF noise; and collective instabilities or insufficient RF acceptance. Mechanical aperture restrictions turn large-amplitude motion into a loss.
Synchrotron-radiation energy loss is normally replenished by RF, so it does not by itself remove one electron for each emitted photon. Rare large energy deviations can nevertheless contribute to losses if they exceed the accepted energy range. Continuous top-up injection can hide the underlying decay and must be accounted for when measuring a lifetime.

At fixed revolution frequency, I=eNfrev​, so a fit to logI versus time gives slope −1/τ for exponential decay. The transformer's zero offset and long-term drift must be controlled, especially at low current. An AC current transformer or a calibrated bunch pickup can additionally resolve bunch charge, whereas a DC transformer provides the total circulating intensity needed here.

Both machines are proposed electron–positron linear colliders, using sources, damping rings, bunch compressors, two opposing main linacs, and final-focus and beam-delivery sections that bring very small bunches to an interaction point. The spent beams go to extraction lines and beam dumps rather than making repeated collision turns.
In the exam-era International Linear Collider reference design, polarized electrons and an undulator-based positron source feed damping rings and two superconducting main linacs; the full 500 GeV centre-of-mass facility is about 31 km long. The Compact Linear Collider adds high-current drive-beam generation and deceleration lines parallel to its main linacs; its 3 TeV concept is roughly 48 km long. The linear layout avoids the repeated synchrotron-radiation losses that would be severe for multi-hundred-GeV electrons in a storage ring. [ref] [ref]

The International Linear Collider uses externally powered superconducting niobium RF cavities at about 1.3 GHz, with a reference average accelerating gradient of 31.5 MV/m. Superconducting walls reduce RF dissipation, allowing relatively long RF pulses and bunch trains, at the cost of cryogenic infrastructure.
The Compact Linear Collider uses normal-conducting copper structures at about 12 GHz and a main-linac gradient near 100 MV/m in its multi-TeV design. A separate high-current, lower-energy electron drive beam is decelerated in power-extraction structures; the resulting RF power accelerates the high-energy, low-current main beams. This two-beam concept supplies short, high-power pulses without requiring a high-power klystron at every main-beam structure.
ILC: superconducting low-loss RF; CLIC: high-gradient normal-conducting two-beam RF. Both rely on damping and final focusing to obtain very small collision spots, so energy alone does not determine their luminosity. [ref] [ref]

Spectral irradiance Fλ​ is radiant power crossing unit area per unit wavelength, integrated over the relevant hemisphere with the projected-area factor: Fλ​=∫Iλ​cosθdΩ. Its units are Wm−2 per unit wavelength; spectral radiance Iλ​ additionally refers to unit solid angle. For an isotropic outgoing hemisphere with Planck function Bλ​, the integral is Fλ​=πBλ​.
The vertical optical depth above height z is the dimensionless extinction integral
τλ​(z)=∫z∞​na​(z′)σλ​(z′)dz′,dzdτλ​​=−na​σλ​=−κλ​ρa​.​
(183)
Here z increases upward, na​ is absorber number density, σλ​ its absorption cross section, ρa​ its mass density, and κλ​ the absorption coefficient per unit absorber mass. Equivalently, using bulk air density ρ and absorber mass fraction qa​, dτλ​/dz=−κλ​qa​ρ. The coefficient may depend on temperature, pressure and wavelength. For purely absorbing gas, transmission along a ray is e−τray​; scattering, if present, contributes to extinction and requires its own source term.

Use the optical-depth weighting stipulated in the paper. A jump in the Planck function at τ1​ gives dB/dτ=(B1​−B0​)δ(τ−τ1​), so
I0​=π[B0​+(B1​−B0​)e−τ1​]=πB0​(1−e−τ1​)+πB1​e−τ1​.​
(184)
The upper isothermal layer emits πB0​(1−e−τ1​) and transmits the lower region's blackbody spectral irradiance with factor e−τ1​. The lower layer and black surface have the same B1​, so their combined radiation entering the upper layer is πB1​, independent of how its emission is divided between the lower gas and surface.
More generally, integration by parts rewrites the supplied expression as
I0​=πB(τs​)e−τs​+π∫0τs​​B(τ)e−τdτ.
(185)
The terms are attenuated surface emission and the atmosphere's own emission. In the original boundary-plus-gradient form, πB0​ is the isothermal reference flux and the integral corrects for temperature variation below the top. Optical depths of order unity contribute most strongly. These formulas follow the paper's specified exponential weighting; a full angular radiative transfer calculation uses ray-angle-dependent optical paths rather than identifying every ray with a vertical path.

Hydrostatic equilibrium balances the vertical pressure gradient against weight, dP/dz=−ρg. For a dry ideal gas parcel displaced slowly enough to maintain pressure balance but rapidly enough to exchange negligible heat, the first law gives
cp​dT−ρ1​dP=0.
(190)
Combining the two equations yields the dry adiabatic lapse rate
Γd​=−dzdT​=cp​g​≃9.8Kkm−1,​
(191)
using cp​≃1004Jkg−1K−1. Here temperature in the thermodynamic differential is absolute, g and cp​ are treated as constant, composition is fixed, and condensation is excluded. Hydrostatic balance alone does not force the atmosphere to be adiabatic; the parcel assumption supplies the extra relation.
Water condensation releases latent heat, reducing the cooling of a rising saturated parcel and giving a smaller moist adiabatic lapse rate. Radiation, mixing, large-scale motion and incomplete convective adjustment also shape the environmental lapse rate. Thus an observed 6--7Kkm−1 need not equal the dry parcel value and is broadly consistent with a moist, radiatively influenced atmosphere.

The equilibrium equation is
(1−βz)(Γz−s)=α,

with roots

a restoring local response requires

The minimum initial height for persistence, a different notion of threshold, is the unstable separator z−​: initial heights above it approach z+​, while lower heights lose ice and leave the model's cold branch. (204)
b1​E0​egt−b0​(C−C0​)=g+b0​Agb0​​(egt−e−b0​t),
(205)
so it satisfies both the differential equation and the initial condition. At t=200 years,
C(2000)=279+0.0350.03e−1+0.005e6​≃336.95ppmv,​
(206)
with E(2000)=0.02e6≃8.069GtCyr−1. The earlier emissions grow on the g−1=33.3 year timescale, much faster than the model's 200-year removal time.

Let t=0 now denote the year 2000 and C00​=336.95ppmv. When emissions stop, the model gives
C(t)=C0​+(C00​−C0​)e−t/(200yr).​
(207)
The concentration peaks at the switch, then returns exponentially to 279ppmv; in 2500 it is about 283.76ppmv. Before 2000 both scenarios share the exponential-emissions trajectory.
Using the specified logarithmic equilibrium warming relative to C0​,
ΔTeq​(C)=3log2​(C/C0​)K,
(208)
gives the fast-adjustment peak estimate
ΔTpeak​≈3log2​(336.95/279)≃0.82K.​
(209)
An unspecified finite thermal response time below twenty years delays and reduces that peak relative to the instantaneous-equilibrium value; its exact amount cannot be fixed without a response law and a chosen thermal time. The carbon-removal time is much longer, so the warming subsequently declines gradually in this model. Taking the 1800 concentration 280 as the temperature reference instead changes the quoted estimate by only 0.016K.

ΔTpeak​⟶3log2​(682.43/279)≃3.87K.​

In 2500 the equilibrium warming is about 3.69K, still below that asymptote. A stable thermal adjustment much faster than the carbon timescale follows this slow approach with a short lag and has the same limiting warming. These are predictions of the specified linear reservoir model, not a claim that constant real emissions produce a finite universal atmospheric equilibrium.

The real carbon cycle has multiple reservoirs and adjustment times, rather than one universally exponential removal process. Air-sea exchange, ocean mixing and carbonate chemistry give a long-lived atmospheric tail; uptake also changes with temperature, circulation and carbon loading. For example, a warming ocean can absorb less additional carbon dioxide, so a fixed b0​ omits a potentially positive climate-carbon feedback. Terrestrial vegetation and soil responses provide further examples. One missing feature is the dependence of carbon uptake on the changing state of the ocean and climate.

1 OurBigBook.com
For a spherical star in hydrostatic equilibrium, dP/dr=−Gm(r)ρ/r2. Multiply by 4πr3dr and integrate to its radius R:
∫0R​4πr3drdP​dr=−∫0R​rGm(r)​dm=Ω.
(213)
Integration by parts gives 4πR3Ps​−3∫PdV=Ω. Neglecting the external surface pressure Ps​, an ideal gas with constant heat capacity ratio γ has thermal energy density u=P/(γ−1). Therefore
3(γ−1)U+Ω=0,U=∫udV.​
(214)
This is the hydrostatic virial theorem. A nonzero confining pressure retains the right-hand side 4πR3Ps​; varying composition, radiation contributions or a spatially varying effective exponent require the integral relation, rather than pulling one γ outside it.

2

Words: 158 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 158
2 OurBigBook.com
For a fully ionized, nonrelativistic monatomic ideal gas, γ=5/3 and the virial theorem becomes
Ω=−2U,E=U+Ω=−U.​
(215)
Since U increases with its particle-weighted mean temperature, the equilibrated self-gravitating object has negative heat capacity: adding total energy allows expansion, makes Ω less negative, and reduces U. Conversely, radiating energy permits contraction and raises the internal temperature. This refers to a sequence of gravitational equilibria, not to the positive local heat capacity of a parcel at fixed volume.
In an ordinary nondegenerate nuclear-burning star, a rise in nuclear heating tends to expand and cool the burning region, lowering its temperature-sensitive reaction rate. Reduced heating leads to contraction and reheating. This expansion feedback is the nuclear thermostat; it can fail in degenerate matter where pressure responds weakly to temperature. During contraction of a pre-main-sequence star, gravitational binding supplies the radiated luminosity and heats the interior. For a fixed-structure scaling, half the released gravitational energy increases U and half escapes as radiation, until hydrogen burning can support a long-lived main sequence equilibrium.

Solution
Words: 209
3 OurBigBook.com
Write Ω=−aGM⊙2​/R⊙​ with a structure factor a of order unity. Then the thermal radiation timescale is
tth​=L⊙​U​=2a​R⊙​L⊙​GM⊙2​​∼107–3×107yr.​
(216)
For a uniform sphere a=3/5, this is about 9.4×106 years. The conventional Kelvin-Helmholtz cooling time GM⊙2​/(R⊙​L⊙​) is about 3.1×107 years; a centrally concentrated solar model changes the coefficient. Both estimates are far shorter than the nuclear lifetime.
Ionization and dissociation can store compression energy without the full temperature rise of a monatomic gas, lowering the effective adiabatic response in partially ionized outer layers. Radiation pressure tends towards an adiabatic exponent 4/3. These effects, changing composition and degeneracy make the effective exponent position dependent. The local dynamical exponent is Γ1​=(∂logP/∂logρ)s​; it equals CP​/CV​ in the simple fixed-composition ideal-gas model, but need not do so for an ionizing mixture.
If an envelope has an effective exponent at or below 4/3, its pressure response is soft and sufficiently extensive such regions can promote radial pulsation, envelope instability or mass loss. In the ideal homologous global model, γ=4/3 is marginal and γ<4/3 is unstable to contraction or expansion. A low value confined to a thin outer layer does not by itself prove collapse of the entire star: global stability depends on the pressure-weighted structure. Its location and mass extent matter.

Solution

Displace a small parcel upward, with negligible heat exchange, rapid pressure balance, and the same composition as its surroundings. Define the environmental gradient ∇=dlogT/dlogP. An adiabatic ideal gas parcel obeys Pρ−γ=constant and hence T∝P(γ−1)/γ, giving ∇ad​=(γ−1)/γ.
The upward displacement has δlogP<0. If ∇<∇ad​, the parcel's temperature changes more negatively than the environment's. At their common pressure it is cooler, denser and driven back down. Therefore the Schwarzschild criterion for stability is
∇=TP​dPdT​<∇ad​=γγ−1​.​
(217)
The reversed inequality produces buoyant growth, and equality is neutrally stable in this approximation. A composition gradient requires the Ledoux criterion; pressure equilibrium alone does not ensure equal mean molecular weight.

In the Sun's cool outer layers, partial ionization lowers the adiabatic temperature gradient, while large opacity makes radiative transport inefficient. The required radiative gradient
∇rad​=16πacGmr​T43κLr​P​
(218)
can exceed ∇ad​, so convection carries part of the outward luminosity. The Sun therefore has an outer convective envelope, above its primarily radiative interior. Here a is the radiation constant, κ opacity per unit mass and mr​,Lr​ the enclosed mass and luminosity. Near the visible surface, radiative losses are again important and the flow need not be perfectly adiabatic.

Solution

b OurBigBook.com
Near a red giant's compact core, intense nuclear burning in a small region can produce a large Lr​/mr​ and a steep required radiative gradient. Where this exceeds the adiabatic gradient, convection transports the released energy and mixes fuel. Core helium burning is a clear example: the strongly temperature-sensitive Triple-alpha process commonly produces a convective burning core; shell flashes can also make convective regions.[ref]
The qualification matters: an inert degenerate helium core and a steady hydrogen-burning shell on the first-ascent red giant branch are not universally convective; conduction or radiation may dominate there. Red giants also commonly have deep convective envelopes. The physical condition is an excessive required radiative gradient, not proximity to the centre alone.

Solution
Words: 245
1 OurBigBook.com
An absorption line depends on the population of its lower atomic level, ionization state, transition strength, pressure and broadening, not just elemental abundance. Boltzmann distribution changes excitation populations with temperature, while the Saha equation changes ionization with temperature and electron pressure. Thus similar overall composition can produce very different spectra. Molecules survive preferentially in cool atmospheres.
The Harvard spectral classification orders the main stellar classes by decreasing effective temperature: O, B, A, F, G, K, M, from blue to red. Numerical subclasses run approximately from 0, the hotter end of a class, to 9, its cooler end. An A0 star, near 104K, has very strong Balmer series lines; hotter stars ionize much of the hydrogen and cooler stars underpopulate its n=2 level. A G2 star, near 5800K, has weaker Balmer absorption, many neutral and ionized metal lines, prominent Ca II H and K lines and the CH G band. An M5 star, near 3000K, has strong TiO molecular bands, neutral-metal and alkali features, and weak photospheric Balmer absorption.[ref]
For giant and dwarf stars of the same colour, compare gravity-sensitive line widths and ratios. The giant's larger radius gives lower surface gravity and atmospheric pressure, typically narrower pressure-broadened lines; high-pressure dwarf atmospheres have stronger broad alkali wings and different molecular and ionization ratios. These diagnostics assign a luminosity class, such as III for a giant and V for a dwarf. A line ratio or calibrated gravity indicator is stronger evidence than colour alone.

Solution
Words: 127
a OurBigBook.com
A 1M⊙​ star spends roughly 1010 years on the main sequence, deriving most of its luminosity from the proton–proton chain. After central hydrogen depletion, shell hydrogen burning around a contracting helium core expands it into a red giant. The low-mass helium core becomes electron-degenerate before the helium flash. Subsequent core helium burning by the Triple-alpha process, with alpha capture producing oxygen, lasts of order 108 years.
After central helium exhaustion, hydrogen and helium shells burn around a carbon-oxygen core on the Asymptotic giant branch. Strong mass loss removes the envelope, potentially making a planetary nebula, and the remnant becomes a carbon-oxygen white dwarf. It cools using stored thermal energy and does not ignite sustained carbon burning. Detailed durations depend on composition and mass loss; the nuclear endpoint of the isolated solar-mass model is a white dwarf.
b
Words: 127 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 127
b OurBigBook.com
A 5M⊙​ star has a much greater luminosity and exhausts central hydrogen in roughly 108 to 2×108 years, mainly through the CNO cycle. It crosses the Hertzsprung gap, develops shell hydrogen burning and ignites core helium without the strongly degenerate helium flash of the solar-mass case. Core helium burning lasts roughly 107 years, with possible blue-loop evolution depending on the model.
It subsequently develops a carbon-oxygen core and double-shell burning on the Asymptotic giant branch, with thermal pulses, winds and envelope loss. For ordinary isolated evolution at this mass, the core does not reach sustained carbon ignition and the final remnant is a carbon-oxygen white dwarf. The broad boundary between white-dwarf and core-collapse outcomes depends on composition, overshooting, rotation and mass loss; the quoted mass is comfortably in the usual intermediate-mass regime.
c
Words: 143 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 143
c OurBigBook.com
A 15M⊙​ star burns core hydrogen chiefly by the CNO cycle for about 107 years. It commonly evolves towards a red supergiant, though winds and mixing alter its track. Core helium burning lasts of order 106 years. Continued contraction then permits carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon burning, producing successively heavier nuclei up to an iron-group core. Neutrino cooling makes the advanced phases much shorter: carbon burning can last thousands of years, while the final burning stages fall to years or days, with substantial model dependence.
An iron-group core cannot gain energy by ordinary fusion into heavier nuclei. Electron captures, photodisintegration and loss of pressure support lead to stellar core collapse. A core-collapse supernova can eject the envelope and leave a neutron star; strong fallback or a failed explosion can instead produce a black hole. The massive-star endpoint involves core collapse, rather than the quiet carbon-oxygen white-dwarf cooling of the two lower-mass examples.

i OurBigBook.com
For a young open cluster, the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram contains a populated main sequence reaching hot, luminous, high-mass stars, with a high-mass main-sequence turnoff determined by its age. Cool low-mass members may still lie on tracks of pre-main-sequence stars above the lower main sequence. Depending on how young the cluster is, a few evolved blue or red supergiants may already be present; an extremely young cluster need not have any. It lacks the dominant old low-mass red-giant and horizontal-branch populations of an old globular cluster.

Solution
Words: 78
ii OurBigBook.com
An old globular cluster has lost its original massive main-sequence members. Its main-sequence turnoff lies near a low stellar mass, typically around 0.8M⊙​ for an age of order 1010 years. The diagram shows a lower main sequence, a subgiant branch, a prominent red giant branch, a horizontal branch of core-helium-burning stars, an Asymptotic giant branch and a faint white dwarf cooling sequence. The preceding schematic labels these features. A few blue stragglers may lie above the old turnoff because interaction or merger rejuvenated them; they do not imply a young age for the bulk population.

Assume homologous, gas-pressure-supported main sequence stars with nearly constant composition and mean molecular weight μ, radiative energy transport and approximately constant opacity κ. Hydrostatic and mass scalings give
Pc​∼R4GM2​,ρc​∼R3M​,Tc​∼kB​Rμmu​GM​.
(219)
The radiative diffusion equation gives the luminosity scaling
L∼κac​ρc​RTc4​​∝κμ4​M3.
(220)
Therefore, under these explicit assumptions,
L∝Mk,k=3.​
(221)
The radius cancels. Radiation-pressure dominance in the most massive stars changes the relation towards the Eddington luminosity scaling L∝M, so the cubic law is an idealized gas-pressure homology result rather than an exact universal massive-star law.

a OurBigBook.com
Face-on, the Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy: a central bulge and bar of scale a few kiloparsecs lie inside a disk of stellar radius roughly 15kpc, with spiral arms containing gas, dust, H II regions and young stars. Recent star formation is concentrated in molecular clouds and arm complexes. The Sun lies in the disk about 8kpc from the centre in the source's convention. Old stars are also present throughout the disk, while the bulge, thick disk and extended stellar halo contain important old populations. Globular clusters occupy a roughly spheroidal halo extending well beyond the bright disk.
b

1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 105
b OurBigBook.com
Edge-on, the bright thin galactic disk forms a narrow band, with a central bulge protruding above and below it and a thinner gas-and-dust lane along the midplane. Young stars and H II regions occupy a vertical scale of a few tenths of a kiloparsec or less; a broader old thick disk has scale of order a kiloparsec. These are approximate scale heights, not sharp boundaries. The old stellar halo and globular clusters form a much larger, low-surface-brightness spheroidal component, extending to many tens of kiloparsecs or more. The dark matter halo is inferred dynamically rather than directly visible in such a sketch. The preceding figure is a structural diagram, not an external photograph or a reconstruction of a particular survey.

Shocks or other ionizing sources can also produce it, but disk star-forming gas is the natural interpretation for an extended spiral-galaxy rotation measurement.
The systemic redshift and inclination of an intrinsically circular thin disk are
z=656.3689.1−656.3​≃0.04998,cosi=307.5​=41​,i≃75.52∘.​

For a spherical mass distribution with constant circular speed vc​,
M(<r)=Gvc2​r​,ρ(r)=4πr21​drdM​=4πGr2vc2​​.​
(232)
For vc​=220kms−1, this is about 0.0140(r/8kpc)−2M⊙​pc−3. It is the spherical model's total density; it is singular if extrapolated to the very centre and is intended only over the flat-rotation region.
For a sharp outer truncation at r∗​, the exterior mass is fixed at M∗​=vc2​r∗​/G. Integrating the gravitational work from r to the boundary and then to infinity gives
21​vesc2​=∫rr∗​​svc2​​ds+∫r∗​∞​s2GM∗​​ds=vc2​[logrr∗​​+1].
(233)
Thus
vesc​(r)=2​vc​1+log(r∗​/r)​.​
(234)
The exterior contribution cannot be dropped: at r=r∗​ it correctly gives the point-mass escape speed 2​vc​.
If the fastest measured radial speed is assumed to approximate both the total speed and the local escape speed of a bound star, then at r=8kpc,
r∗​≃rexp(2(220)24302​−1)≃19.9kpc.​
(235)
Without those extra assumptions, the measurement gives only a bound: a bound star's total speed is at least its radial component, and the sample maximum need not reach escape, so r∗​≳19.9kpc within this model. An unbound interloper would invalidate even that bound. This is not a determination of the real Milky Way halo edge.
